msg: Paper 114 shows that although Urantia is a planet isolated by rebellion, it has never been abandoned. The Most Highs rule in the kingdoms of men through many celestial forces, but chiefly through the ministry of the seraphim, and the master seraphim of planetary supervision, divided into twelve groups such as the epochal angels, the progress angels, the religious guardians, and the angels of nation life, watch over the civilization, religion, and society of mankind. Today's passage tells us that, aside from these many forms of positive action, there is yet another safeguard: the reserve corps of destiny.

The reserve corps of destiny is made up of living men and women, people whom the celestial forces have held in readiness against emergencies so as to insure against the breakdown of evolutionary progress. The passage calls them the provisions made against surprise, the guarantees against disaster. The seventh section of the same paper explains that these people usually live ordinary lives without being conscious of their role, and that they are prepared through their special ability to cooperate with the Thought Adjuster and through the help of the midwayers. When a moment of crisis comes, the understanding and judgment planted in their minds beforehand come into play and keep civilization from sliding into catastrophe.

This teaching renews the way we look at history. When we hear the news of the world, mankind's future often seems precarious. But the rule of the Universal Father works more through quiet preparation than through dramatic miracles. Heaven raises up people in advance and stores within their characters the wisdom to withstand a crisis. Evolution is slow and at times seems to slip backward, yet beneath it lies an unseen safety net that keeps it from collapse. Trust, therefore, rather than fear, is the attitude that befits us.

At the same time, this passage quietly puts a question to each of us. Belonging to the reserve corps is not something we can decide for ourselves, but the way to become a person fit for such service is open to everyone. Those who open their hearts to the indwelling Adjuster, who carry out their daily responsibilities with honesty and loyalty, and who put the welfare of the community ahead of their own interest are people heaven can call upon when needed. The wisdom used in a crisis does not suddenly appear in the crisis. It accumulates little by little in a faithful everyday life and grows firm in the habit of making small decisions rightly.

Here we see the deep respect contained in the way heaven works. The celestial forces do not ignore human free will and forcibly manipulate events. Instead, they work through human beings and with them. What averts a crisis is not lightning from heaven but the calm judgment and courageous action of a prepared person. In this way God does not keep his children merely as objects of protection but establishes them as co-workers who share in the destiny of their world.

Today, it would be good to remember two things. One is that this world is under celestial watchcare and that the progress of mankind is never left defenseless. The other is that we ourselves can become hands of that care. Even without a grand mission, holding up what is about to collapse and steadying those who are faltering in our homes, workplaces, and neighborhoods is work that shares the spirit of the reserve corps of destiny. May this be a day in which, willing to be used in heaven's plan, we faithfully keep the post entrusted to us today.
d223.pr: Choose one thing at your post today that must be held up so it does not collapse, and faithfully keep it.

msg: The final paragraph of Paper 114 closes the whole paper with warm comfort. Earlier the author described the intricate administration that watches over this world: the sovereignty of Urantia, the board of planetary supervisors, the resident governor general, the Most High observer, and on to the master seraphim and the reserve corps of destiny. At the end of all these explanations he states one thing plainly: your isolated world is not forgotten in the counsels of the universe.

Urantia was cut off from the spiritual circuits of the system by the Lucifer rebellion and the betrayal of Caligastia. Add to this the default of Adam and Eve, and this planet long went without the benefits that normal evolutionary worlds enjoy. Are we, then, abandoned orphans of the universe? The passage answers with a firm no. From Uversa to Salvington and on down to Jerusem, even in Havona and on Paradise, they all know we are here. Indeed, the mortals of this world are just as lovingly cherished as if the sphere had never been betrayed by a faithless Planetary Prince, even more so.

Why even more so? Just as a parent's heart leans more toward a child in trouble, the watchcare of the universe dwells more deeply where the need is greater. That Michael chose this very confused world as the stage for his final bestowal bears witness to this (see Paper 119). Isolation has become not a sign of heaven's indifference but rather a stage on which special mercy and special ministry unfold. The Thought Adjuster indwelling each of us and the poured-out Spirit of Truth are the nearest proofs that this world has not been abandoned.

This truth applies just as well to our personal lives. In failure and loss we sometimes feel that heaven has forgotten us. Our prayers seem to come back without an echo, and a loneliness, as though we had been left alone, sweeps over us. But if a whole planet was not forgotten even in its isolation, a single soul living on that planet cannot be forgotten. It is eternally true, “⟦Q 114:7.17⟧the Father himself loves you,⟦/Q⟧” and it remains unchangeably true even in moments when our feelings cannot sense it.

This comfort is not sentimental talk; it rests on the facts this paper sets out in detail. The Most High observer watches over planetary crises with authority to intervene when necessary, and the twenty-four counselors, who know this world's circumstances better than anyone, assist in planetary administration. Countless seraphim work unceasingly for the progress of mankind, and the reserve corps of destiny stands ready to keep civilization from collapsing. When we know that so many beings are working unseen for this small world, we realize that we are never alone. Moreover, this love is unconditional. Urantia is not loved because it has done well; it is loved even though the leaders of this world failed. Likewise, each of us is loved not because we are perfect but because we are children of God. Our faults and weaknesses are not reasons for heaven to withdraw its concern but channels through which greater mercy flows in.

So today we are invited to lay down an orphan consciousness and live with the consciousness of a child. The assurance that heaven knows me, remembers my name and my path, and lovingly watches every step I take changes the way we live. Peace takes the place of anxiety, and courage the place of resignation. And one who is loved in this way can become a channel who goes to neighbors feeling lonely and forgotten and lets them know that they, too, are never forgotten.
d224.pr: Several times today, quietly turn over the truth that the Father himself loves you, and engrave it on your heart.

msg: Before treating the Supreme Being, Paper 115 first speaks of the relativity of conceptual frames. A partial, incomplete, and evolving intellect cannot understand everything at once, so when it thinks about the universe it must set up some frame and think within it. Today's passage says that these frames are only relatively true; they are serviceable scaffolding which must eventually give way before the expansions of enlarging cosmic comprehension.

What is remarkable is that this relativity extends to our understandings of truth, beauty, goodness, love, and even Deity. This does not mean that truth itself wavers. God is unchangeably real, and his goodness does not change. It means only that the concepts by which we grasp them are always partial. The passage says that God is much, much more than a Father, but the Father is man's highest concept of God. Jesus' revelation of God as Father was the noblest gift that could be given to mortals.

Yet the passage also tells us that even this Father-Son concept will be augmented by broader supermortal conceptions in Orvonton, in Havona, and on Paradise. The ascending journey is a journey of endless learning. Our understanding of God today will grow larger and deeper tomorrow, and that growth does not discard the earlier understanding but builds a higher story upon it. Scaffolding is indispensable for constructing a building, but as the building rises, new scaffolding must be set up higher.

This teaching offers two lessons for our life of faith. The first is humility. To regard my concept of God as complete and to judge the understanding of others carelessly is to forget the relativity of concepts. Religious self-righteousness usually arises from mistaking the scaffolding for the building. The second is open-mindedness. Those who do not fear new insights when they come, but gladly welcome them, grow spiritually. The passage's words, that man must think in a mortal universe frame but that this does not mean he cannot envision other and higher frames, are an encouragement to widen the horizon of our thought.

The fact that concepts are relative does not throw us into confusion. Rather, it encourages us to live out faithfully the understanding we have now. That today's scaffolding will someday be replaced does not make it useless. When we hold to the highest concept given to us today, God as our loving Father, and live in keeping with it, we become ready to receive the next, broader understanding. Truth opens more deeply when it is lived out than when it is merely arranged in the head. The Urantia Book itself shows this principle. The revelators present concepts suited to the level of human understanding, and they state repeatedly that these are not final statements but the frames most helpful to the people of this age (see Paper 0). This is why, when we read the revelation, we must not be imprisoned by the letter but must seek the living meaning within it.

Today we are invited to treasure the intimate relationship of calling God our Father while remembering that he is greater than all our concepts. When we pray, let us fully enjoy the love and trust contained in the name Father, yet never lose our reverence before the infinite One who is beyond that name. When we do so, our faith will become not a hardened frame but a living experience that grows day by day.
d225.pr: Recall one idea about God that you hold firmly, and meditate on whether there is a way to understand it more broadly.

d226.t: Not an Ending but a Transition
msg: The third section of Paper 115 explains reality through three categories, the original, the actual, and the potential, and shows the growth of the universe as it unfolds in time. Today's passage, the last paragraph of that section, closes with a simple yet profound insight. From a circumscribed view there are, indeed, many ends, many terminations of activities, but from a larger viewpoint on a higher universe level, there are no endings, merely transitions from one phase of development to another.

The major chronicity of the master universe is divided into great ages: the Havona, the superuniverse, and the outer universe ages. But the passage says that even these basic divisions cannot be more than relative landmarks on the unending highway of eternity. Landmarks keep us from losing our way, but they do not mark the end of the road. The history of the universe is not a story that closes but a story that keeps unfolding, and whenever one chapter ends, a new chapter always begins.

This cosmic perspective offers great comfort for our personal lives. We experience many endings in life. We finish school, leave jobs, see relationships end, and part from those we love. And someday this life in the flesh will end as well. But the Urantia Book teaches that even mortal death is not an ending but a transition. The surviving soul awakens on the mansion worlds, continues the morontia career, and keeps walking the long ascending path toward Paradise (see Paper 47). A soul formed together with the Thought Adjuster never returns to nothingness.

So in moments that look like endings, we can look for the seeds of a new beginning. When one phase closes, the experience and wisdom gained within it do not vanish but become the foundation of the next phase. For one who walks with God, even failed plans and lost opportunities become material for growth. One who knows this does not clutch too tightly in the face of change and can let go with gratitude of what must be let go.

This truth is confirmed not only on the cosmic scale but also in the small routines of each day. When the day fades, night comes, and when the night passes, a new morning dawns. Winter looks like an ending, yet beneath the ground it is preparing for spring. Even the cycles of nature quietly teach the cosmic principle that there are no endings, only transitions. So it is with our spiritual life as well. A season of dryness may not be an ending but a time of preparation for deeper experience. This teaching also tells us what we should be building as we live. What passes over with us when the phases change is not possessions or position but experience, character, and spiritual values. Material things are left behind at the end of a phase, but deeds done in love and choices made for truth are preserved in the soul and carried on to the next stage. So one who walks the highway of eternity sets the heart on what will remain rather than on what will pass away.

If there is an ending before us today, let us see it as a landmark on the highway of eternity. Sorrow is natural, but despair is unnecessary. In the plan of the Universal Father, everything is moving forward, and we too are moving on toward higher phases. The truth that there are no endings promises us endless growth and endless hope.
d226.pr: Recall one ending you have recently gone through, and write down what new beginning it is leading to.

msg: Paper 116 deals with the Almighty Supreme, the power and mind of the Supreme Being who is evolving in the universes of time and space. The first section speaks of the Supreme Mind, and in today's passage the author candidly confesses that we really know less about the mind of Supremacy than about any other aspect of this evolving Deity. Yet even amid that uncertainty, he says, one thing is clear: mind never ceases to progress.

The passage compares physique, spirit, and mind. Physique may attain completed growth; our bodies stop growing at a certain age. Spirit may achieve perfection of development. But mind is the experiential technique of endless progress. Mind bridges matter and spirit, links facts with meanings and values, and ceaselessly learns and integrates what is new. That is why, the passage says, the Supreme, being an experiential Deity, never achieves completion of mind attainment.

These words give us great hope. The body ages and strength declines, but the growth of mind has no age limit. Someone past seventy can still grasp a new truth, learn a new way of loving, and lay down old prejudices. The whole ascending career is built on this very endless progress of mind. On the mansion worlds, in the local universe, in the superuniverse and Havona, we will keep on learning and growing. A person who has stopped learning, though still alive, has closed the door of growth with his own hand.

At the same time, this teaching poses a practical challenge for our daily lives. For the mind to progress, we must keep it open. The comfort of staying with familiar thoughts, the conceit of thinking we already know it all, and fear of new experience all block the progress of mind. Curiosity, humility, and the habit of asking questions, on the other hand, move the mind forward. The Thought Adjuster works within our minds, ceaselessly presenting higher concepts and ideals, but receiving and choosing them is our part.

The progress of mind is not simply a matter of adding knowledge. It is the growth of the ability to raise facts into meanings and meanings into values. One who knows a great deal of information is not necessarily wise. True growth of mind shows itself in rightly connecting what one knows and translating it into life's choices and acts of love. That is why the Urantia Book places wisdom above knowledge, and spiritual insight above wisdom. And the endless progress of mind also means that we will never face a boring eternity. Some worry that eternal life might be a monotonous state of endless repetition. But in a universe where mind never stops, new discoveries and new adventures always lie ahead. Eternity is not stagnation but endless growth.

The growth of each of our minds does not end as a merely personal matter. The experience of evolving creatures actually contributes to the growth of the Supreme Being (see Paper 117). So one small truth we learn today, one thought we rightly set in order, carries cosmic significance. Remembering the truth that mind never stops, let us live today as learners.
d227.pr: Choose one thing you would like to learn today, and take time to explore it with an open mind.

msg: The final section of Paper 116 describes the grand universe as a living organism. This vast universe, woven of matter, mind, and spirit, is at once a mechanism and something like a living body, in which every part is interconnected and grows together. Today's passage speaks of the divinity tension that arises within this living cosmos. Its source is none other than man's urge for Paradise perfection, his striving for God-attainment.

The word tension often sounds negative, but here it means a holy force that draws life forward. Just as an arrow flies only when the bowstring is drawn, the distance between who I am now and who I am meant to become causes me to grow. The passage says that this tension can only be resolved by the evolution of an immortal soul. In other words, as we seek God, choose to do his will, and grow in soul, this holy longing is gradually realized and fulfilled.

The passage goes a step further. What happens within a single person is happening at the same time within all creatures and all Creators in the grand universe. When all beings strive for God-attainment and divine perfection, there is built up a profound cosmic tension which can only find resolution in the sublime synthesis of almighty power with the spirit person of the Supreme Being. Our spiritual longing is part of the longing carried by the whole universe, and our growth joins the vast current of the completion of the Supreme.

This teaching lets us see spiritual dissatisfaction in a new light. Sometimes we feel frustrated, asking why we have gotten only this far. But that holy discontent is itself evidence that a longing for God is alive within us. It is not a reason for discouragement but a reason to keep going. We must only take care that this tension does not turn into impatience or self-reproach. The evolution of the soul takes time, and the Thought Adjuster works with us patiently.

We can feel this tension within ourselves as well. Within us are both the pull of our animal nature and the call of spiritual ideals. The desire for comfort and the desire to reach for something higher pull against each other and test us. This tension shows that we are not yet complete, but it also shows that we are called to completion. A life with no tension at all may look peaceful, but in fact it may be a life in which growth has stopped. The Urantia Book teaches that the way to resolve this tension lies not in forcibly eliminating conflict but in choosing again and again to do the Father's will. As those choices accumulate, the soul grows, and inner conflict gradually turns into harmony. This is a small completion achieved within one person, and such completions together make up the great completion of the Supreme.

Today, let us treasure the desire within us to become better and the longing to know God more. It is part of the divinity tension that keeps the universe alive. And when we remember that this longing is not ours alone but one we share with all creatures, we can walk the path without loneliness. All beings are moving together toward perfection.
d228.pr: Recall one longing within you to become better, and take a small step in that direction today.

d229.t: The More We Love, the More Real We Become
msg: Paper 117 speaks of God the Supreme, the experiential Deity who is evolving in the creations of time and space. The fourth section calls him the finite God and reveals the astonishing fact that his growth actually depends on the choices and experiences of finite creatures. Today's passage, the last paragraph of that section, sums up the whole discussion in one profound mystery: the more closely man approaches God through love, the greater the reality, the actuality, of that man.

The passage first says that God's gifts, his bestowal of reality, are not divorcements from himself. God does not alienate creation from himself and leave it on its own; he has set up tensions in the creations circling Paradise. That tension is a pull that draws every creature back to its source. And the order is clear. God first loves man and confers upon him the potential of immortality. As man responds to that love and loves God, that potential becomes actual. Eternal life blossoms where the possibility God has given meets the response of man.

This overturns our thinking about existence. We usually assume that I already exist and that afterward I enter into a relationship with God. But the passage says that the deeper the relationship with God becomes, the more real a being I become. Conversely, the more man withdraws from God, the more nearly he approaches nonreality, cessation of existence. A life that rejects God is not merely a morally wrong life; it is a life that grows ever thinner and loses its reality. For God is the source of all reality.

How, then, can we draw near to God? The passage offers a clear way. When man consecrates his will to the doing of the Father's will, when man gives God all that he has, then does God make that man more than he is. Here lies the paradox of the spiritual life. The one who lets go of self becomes greater, while the one who clings to self grows ever smaller. Jesus' teaching that whoever loses his life shall find it reveals this same principle.

This consecration is not finished in a single dramatic decision. It is carried out in the small choices of every day. As we choose to respond with love when we are angry, choose honesty between the selfish way and the honest way, and build the habit of asking first for the Father's will rather than our own plans, we become, little by little, more real beings. The indwelling Thought Adjuster transforms all these choices into eternal values and preserves them in the soul. This teaching shows that the relationship between God and man is not one-sided. God loves us even when we do not respond, but for that love to bear fruit in us as eternal reality, our love is needed. Because love cannot be forced, God waits for our free response. He respects that response and, through it, raises us up as co-workers who create together with him.

Today we are invited to lay down the urge to clutch what we have and to come one step closer to God in love. Giving to God is not losing; it is the way to receive a greater self. God loved us first, so all we need do is respond to that love. In that response we grow into beings who are eternally real.
d229.pr: Entrust to God one thing you have been holding on to today, and quietly choose to follow his will.

d230.t: Love Lives Only When It Flows
msg: The sixth section of Paper 117 deals with the quest for the Supreme, how we may find God the Supreme. In the preceding paragraph the author said that God is the greatest experience in human existence and that finding God is an act of freely bestowing love. Today's passage beautifully shows where that love comes from and where it flows. All true love is from God, and man receives the divine affection as he himself bestows this love upon his fellows.

The heart of the passage is that love is dynamic. It can never be captured; it is alive, free, thrilling, and always moving. Man can never take the love of the Father and imprison it within his heart. Just as standing water goes stale, love that does not flow is no longer love. The Father's love can become real to mortal man only by passing through that man's personality as he in turn bestows this love upon his fellows. Love is not something to possess but something to pass on.

The passage calls this the great circuit of love. Love is from the Father, through sons to brothers, and hence to the Supreme. The love of the Father appears in the mortal personality by the ministry of the indwelling Adjuster, and the God-knowing son reveals this love to his universe brethren. And this fraternal affection, the passage says, is the essence of the love of the Supreme. When we love our neighbors, we are taking part in the growth of God the Supreme.

This teaching explains why Jesus never separated the love of God from the love of neighbor. One who claims to love God while remaining cold toward neighbors has blocked the circuit. In such a person even the love of God cannot become real. Conversely, one who lets love flow through small kindnesses, patience, and forgiveness receives more love in the process. This mystery, that the giver receives, is the very nature of the circuit of love. What does this look like in real life? When our hearts are dry and we cannot feel love, we often try to fill up on love first and then share it. But the passage teaches the reverse: when we begin to share love, love fills us as it passes through us. Small acts such as checking on someone who is lonely, lightening the load of a weary colleague, or praying for someone who has hurt us reopen a circuit that had been blocked.

This circuit does not operate only in grand undertakings. Rather, love flows most through the trivial moments of ordinary life. A warm word to a family member, courtesy shown to a stranger, generosity that covers a colleague's mistake: all of these are channels through which the Father's love flows. Even when we are not aware of it, such small acts join the great current running from the Father through the brothers to the Supreme. So no love is small or wasted.

Today we are called to be not reservoirs of love but channels of love. Because the love that comes from the Father is endless, it does not run short when we let it flow out. On the contrary, the more we let it flow, the wider the channel becomes and the more love flows through it. In that flow we come to know God, to know our brothers, and to experience the love of the Supreme.
d230.pr: Today, show one specific small kindness to someone to whom you have found it hard to express love.

msg: Paper 118 is a difficult paper that explains the Supreme and the Ultimate in terms of time and space, but its first section, through the theme of time and eternity, offers teaching that touches our spiritual lives directly. Today's passage tells how the mortal creature may become eternal. The way is self-identification with the indwelling spirit through the technique of choosing to do the will of the Father.

The passage explains that such a consecration of will is tantamount to the realization of eternity-reality of purpose. When we sincerely decide to do the Father's will, that purpose becomes something that does not waver with the passage of time. Whether a million or a billion moments go by, that purpose does not change. Number has ceased to have meaning. A being who lives in time comes to hold something that transcends time: this is the beginning of eternal life. These words tell us that eternity is not only a matter of the distant future. We often think of eternal life as an endlessly long stretch of time that begins after death. But according to the passage, eternity is not a length of time but a quality of purpose. The moment our decision to do the Father's will becomes firm, we have already set foot in what is eternal. Jesus' saying that knowing God is eternal life points to the same truth.

The last sentence of the passage is even more beautiful. Creature choice plus God's choice eventuate in the eternal realities of the never-ending union of the spirit of God and the nature of man. The Thought Adjuster is spirit that comes from God, and our will is the noblest part of human nature. When these two face the same direction, a new being is born of their union: a soul that survives eternally. This is not something we can do alone, nor something God does without us.

So what matters most for us today is our choice. God has already chosen on his side. He has sent the Adjuster to dwell within us and has opened the door of eternal life. What remains now is our response. That response is not a grand vow but small decisions repeated in daily life. Each time we decide what to say, how to work, and how to treat whom, asking for the Father's will is itself a choice toward eternity.

Let us notice here the word technique. Choosing to do the Father's will is less a mystical experience completed at a single stroke than a skill of living learned through repeated practice. At first we are clumsy and often stumble, but the more we repeat it, the more natural and deeper that choice becomes. Just as one learning an instrument practices every day, the spiritual person practices choosing the Father's will every day. A will refined in this way finally becomes an unwavering purpose and forms an eternal reality that transcends time.

One whose purpose to do the Father's will is fixed, even amid fickle emotions and shifting circumstances, enjoys a deep inner stability, because time cannot shake that person. As we begin this day, let us consecrate that purpose anew. In that choice, eternity has already begun to grow within us.
d231.pr: As you begin the day, confess in your heart that you want to do the Father's will, and look back on the day in the evening.

msg: The final section of Paper 118 deals with the function of providence. Many people think of providence as God having arranged everything for us in advance, or as a special intervention that changes our circumstances when we pray. This section corrects such ideas and reveals the true nature of providence. Today's passage, its conclusion, tells us what happens when we pray for providential intervention amid life's difficulties.

The passage first says this: many times the answer to such prayer is their own changed attitudes toward life. We pray for our circumstances to change, but God often changes us before he changes our circumstances. The problem remains, but the eyes that look at it are different; the burden remains, but strength to carry it arises. This does not mean the prayer went unanswered; it was answered at a deeper level. For circumstances pass, but a changed attitude remains in the soul forever.

The passage then stresses that providence is not whimsical, neither is it fantastic nor magical. Providence is the slow and sure emergence of the mighty sovereign of the finite universes, the Supreme Being. It is the sure and certain march of the galaxies of space and the personalities of time toward the goals of eternity, first in the Supreme, then in the Ultimate. Providence is not a device for granting individual wishes but a vast current leading the whole universe toward good purposes. The earlier part of this section also says that providence functions with regard to the function of the part within the whole rather than the importance of the individual.

This holds an important lesson for our life of prayer. Prayer is not an attempt to change God's mind. God already loves us perfectly and wants what is best. Prayer is rather the process of attuning ourselves to God's will (see Paper 91). So a prayer that asks how I should grow in this situation is more mature than a prayer that only asks for things. Such a prayer is always answered.

Of course, this does not mean we should not bring our specific needs to God in prayer. As a child pours out his heart to his father, we too can tell him everything. But when we leave the outcome to God and do not dictate the form of the answer, prayer brings peace. And in that process we learn to see life differently. When resentment turns to gratitude, fear to trust, and impatience to patience, that is the clearest sign of providence at work within us. The passage also says that in infinity we believe there is the same providence, the will, the actions, the purpose of the Paradise Trinity motivating the cosmic panorama of universes upon universes. Our small lives are set within this vast purpose. Even if not all our personal wishes come true, our lives are not left to chance but are part of a universe guided by love and wisdom. This trust sets us free from worry.

If there is a problem we are holding on to in prayer today, let us bring it to God and offer him our own attitude as well. When we pray not only that our circumstances be changed but also that we ourselves be changed, we will experience the slow but sure touch of providence.
d232.pr: Thinking of the problem you are praying about now, ask what attitude of yours needs to change in the face of it.

msg: Paper 119 tells of the seven bestowals of Christ Michael. Michael, the Creator Son of our local universe of Nebadon, incarnated seven times in the likeness of the beings he had created, and the last of these was his coming on Urantia as Jesus, the Son of Man. Today's passage, the opening of this paper, briefly explains the purpose of these creature incarnations: to enable such Creators to become wise, sympathetic, just, and understanding sovereigns.

The most striking expression in the passage is this: these divine Sons are innately just, but they become understandingly merciful as a result of these successive bestowal experiences; they are naturally merciful, but these experiences make them merciful in new and additional ways. The Creator Son is good and merciful from the very beginning, yet by actually living the life of a creature, his mercy acquires the depth of experience. Mercy that knows is different from mercy that has lived through it.

This teaching gives great comfort about how God deals with us. Michael, our sovereign, does not know only in his head what kind of beings we are. He was actually born as a baby and grew up; he bore poverty and the responsibilities of a family; he was misunderstood, rejected, and finally met death on the cross. That is why he fully understands our weaknesses. When we come before him, we stand not before a ruler who judges from afar but before a brother and father who has walked the same road.

The passage calls these bestowals the last steps in the Creator Son's education and training. The fact that even a Creator of infinite power learns through experience shows how precious experience is in the universe. It teaches us the same principle. The difficulties and pains we go through are not in vain. Through them we learn a heart that understands others, a heart that sympathizes before it judges. This is why the comfort of one who has passed through suffering runs deep. So we, too, can follow Michael's path and learn understanding mercy. When we see someone's mistake, let us not measure it by principle alone but try to stand in that person's place. Justice is important, but justice without understanding easily turns cold. Conversely, mercy without justice easily turns soft. What Michael gained through his bestowals was a character in which these two are blended into one: wise and sympathetic rule.

Through his seven bestowals Michael lived, in turn, the life of a Melchizedek Son, a Lanonandek Son, a Material Son, a seraphim, an ascending spirit, a morontia mortal, and finally a mortal man. In each bestowal he personally experienced how beings of a different order view the universe and what difficulties and joys they go through. So his sovereignty rests not only on authority conferred from above but on understanding gained from below. Because he is such a ruler, every being in his universe can trust him completely.

Today each of us also holds some small rule at home and at work. As parents, colleagues, and neighbors, we stand in places where we judge others and make decisions. Each time, may we remember Michael's bestowals and act justly and mercifully, with a heart that seeks to understand the other person's life.
d233.pr: If there is someone you feel like judging today, first try to see the situation from that person's place.

msg: The final section of Paper 119 explains Michael's status after completing all seven bestowals. He has now become the settled sovereign of Nebadon, and having passed through the experience of revealing the will of the Seven Master Spirits, he has attained sevenfold sovereignty. Today's passage shows the place our small world, Urantia, holds in this great journey. Urantia is the sentimental shrine of all Nebadon, the chief of ten million inhabited worlds.

The passage lists Michael's many names at length: a Melchizedek minister to the realms, a system savior, an Adamic redeemer, a seraphic fellow, an associate of ascending spirits, a morontia progressor, a Son of Man in the likeness of mortal flesh, and the Planetary Prince of Urantia. These names sum up the seven bestowals he passed through. And the last chapter of that whole journey was written on this very world. Urantia became his mortal home. Urantia is called a shrine not because this world is especially excellent. On the contrary, it was a confused planet wounded by rebellion and default. But it was in just such a place that the Creator lived in the lowliest form, revealed the deepest love, and ended his life on the cross. That is why this world has become a place that all Nebadon regards with emotion and awe. The wounded place has become the holiest place.

The last sentence of the passage awakens our hope. Jesus has promised sometime to return to the world of his terminal bestowal, the World of the Cross. No one knows when or how he will come, but that promise shows that this world has never left his heart (see Paper 176). We live not in a world he has left behind but in a world to which he has promised to return. And in the meantime he has sent the Spirit of Truth to abide with every person.

This fact gives us who live as people of Urantia a special meaning and responsibility. We live on the land the Creator himself walked, under the same sky he gazed upon, where he broke bread with others. If we remember this, we cannot treat this world carelessly, nor can we take lightly the neighbors who live in it. For people like those Jesus loved are living beside us now.

Come to think of it, this resembles our own journey of faith. God does not avoid our weakest and most shameful parts; rather, it is there that he bestows his deepest grace. The wounded places of our lives, the places of failure and tears, sometimes become the places where we have met God most closely. Just as Urantia became the shrine of Nebadon, the dark moments of our lives can also become shrines that bear witness to God's love. He discards nothing and redeems everything. We should also remember that the experience Michael gained on this world was for his whole universe. The life he lived on Urantia became an inspiration and a revelation to all the inhabited worlds of Nebadon. So this small planet is by no means a small place.

Today, let us look with new eyes at the land and the age in which we live. This is not a forgotten backwater but a sentimental shrine of the universe. May this be a day in which, as befits those who live in that shrine, we reveal in our daily lives the love and truth Jesus showed us.
d234.pr: Give thanks today as you recall, over the roads you walk and the people you meet, the holiness of this world where Jesus walked.

msg: Paper 120 records the words of commission spoken to Michael, just before he began his Urantia bestowal, by his brother Immanuel, the Union of Days. Immanuel, as the Union of Days in Nebadon, promised to take charge of its administration while Michael was away from his universe and gave him the counsel needed for his final bestowal. Today's passage contains the heart of that commission.

Immanuel says: “⟦Q 120:1.4⟧Throughout your Urantia bestowal you need be concerned with but one thing, the unbroken communion between you and your Paradise Father.⟦/Q⟧” The task given to the mighty Creator Son who creates and rules a universe is astonishingly simple. Planetary politics, universe administration, and the adjudication of rebellion were not his chief concern. The one thing he had to hold fast was his relationship with the Father. And within that simplicity lies a wonderful promise: by the perfection of such a relationship the world of his bestowal, even all the universe of his creation, will behold a new and more understandable revelation of the Universal Father. The power by which Jesus' life changed the world came not from dazzling miracles or political achievements but flowed from his unbroken communion with the Father. A life at one with the Father was itself the most powerful revelation.

Immanuel also adds that Michael's concern has only to do with his personal life on Urantia. He promises to be responsible himself for the security and administration of the universe. Michael could lay down his concern for the universe and devote himself wholly to living as a man who does the Father's will. The greater one's responsibilities, the more one can be faithful to what matters most by laying down what should be laid down. These words apply to us today just as they are. Our lives are full of things to do and things to worry about. Family, work, health, finances, and the problems of society constantly demand our attention. Amid it all, it is easy to forget what matters most. But Jesus' life teaches clearly that everything else falls into place when it finds its order around the center of communion with the Father.

Jesus' words, seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, express the same principle. One who puts the relationship with the Father first does not neglect other things but rather handles them more rightly, because wisdom, peace, and strength flow from that relationship. Doing a little while connected to the Father bears greater fruit than doing much while cut off from him. Let us also remember that there are burdens we, too, can lay down. We do not need to hold up the universe by our own strength. We can entrust to the Father what we cannot be fully responsible for and be faithful to the life we are to live here and now. That is the path Michael walked, and the path we, his children, are to follow.

This communion does not take place only in special places or at special times. Jesus never broke off his communion with the Father, whether he was doing carpentry, caring for his family, or teaching the multitudes. For him prayer was not one part of the day but like a breath that enfolded his whole life.

Today, amid many tasks, let us make our greatest concern not to break our communion with the Father. May it be a day of walking with him, speaking to the Father in a corner of the heart even while we work and meet people.
d235.pr: Pause three times between your tasks today to speak briefly to the Father and keep your communion unbroken.

msg: Before telling the life of Jesus in earnest, Paper 121 explains the background of the age into which he was born. The midwayer author introduces in turn the Occidental world, the Jewish people, and the philosophies and religions of the gentiles, helping us understand why Michael came at just that time and place. Today's passage, its first paragraph, opens with an astonishing statement: Jesus did not come to this world during an age of spiritual decadence.

People often think that Jesus came in the darkest and most corrupt of times. But the passage says the very opposite. At the time of his birth Urantia was experiencing such a revival of spiritual thinking and religious living as it had not known in all its previous post-Adamic history. The world presented the most favorable condition for the Creator Son's bestowal that had ever previously prevailed or has since obtained. God does not choose his time at random; he waits for the most fitting time. The passage lists these favorable conditions specifically. Greek culture and the Greek language had spread over the Occident and the near Orient, so that new ideas could travel across borders. The Jews, a Levantine race in nature part Occidental and part Oriental, were eminently fitted to spread a new religion to both East and West. In addition, the tolerant political rule of the Romans bound the Mediterranean world together, providing roads and peace. A later part of this paper sums it up: Greece supplied the language, Rome the roads, and the Jews the monotheistic faith.

This gives deep insight into the way God works. God does not work by ignoring the course of history. Rather, he waits for the culture, language, and politics of mankind to ripen, and he works through them. When Paul said that in the fullness of time God sent forth his Son, he was pointing to just this completion of preparation. Great revelation comes when there are minds prepared to receive it and channels prepared to carry it. This principle applies to our personal lives as well. We often ask why God does not answer now, why he makes us wait. But God may be waiting for readiness to ripen within us. Some truths come to us only when we have grown enough to bear them. A season of waiting is not wasted time but a time of preparation.

At the same time, this passage prompts us to look at our own age. Today, too, the world is bound together by travel and communication, and many people long for genuine spiritual experience beyond formal religion. This may be a favorable condition for the original gospel of Jesus, the simple truth that God is our Father and all men are brothers, to be proclaimed anew (see Paper 195). Then what part can we play in this prepared age? Just as the Greek language and the Roman roads became channels for the gospel, the languages, relationships, and talents we possess can also become channels of truth. Even without starting a grand movement, one person who lives out the spirit of Jesus is taking part in God's preparation for that age.

In this way God's plan ripens quietly over long ages. Ever since Melchizedek sowed the seeds of monotheism, countless prophets and teachers prepared the way, and at last, when everything was ready, Michael came.
Today we are called to trust God's timing while faithfully living the time given to us. God always works at the most fitting time, and he calls us to be co-workers in that work.
d236.pr: Recall one matter in your life for which you are waiting on God's timing, and consider what preparation you can make now.

d237.t: Hunger for the Bread of Life
msg: The fifth section of Paper 121 introduces the religions of the gentiles in Jesus' day. Alongside state worship, emperor worship, and various schools of philosophy, the mystery religions were enormously popular in the Roman Empire. Mystery cults such as the Phrygian cult of the Great Mother, the Egyptian rites of Isis and Osiris, and Mithraism from Persia captured the hearts of many. Today's passage clearly sets out the relationship between these mystery religions and the teachings of Jesus.

The passage first warns: do not make the mistake of confusing the teachings of Jesus with the mysteries. The gospel of Jesus was not a religion of salvation through secret rites or initiation procedures. It was the simple and open truth that every person can become a child of God by faith. The mystery religions stirred the emotions through myths of a dying and rising god and through elaborate ceremonies, but Jesus taught a living, personal relationship with the Father in heaven. Yet the passage does not simply disparage the mystery religions. Rather, it says that their popularity reveals man's quest for survival. People flocked to the mystery cults because of a longing for life beyond death, a real hunger and thirst for personal religion and individual righteousness. State religion and cold philosophy could not satisfy that longing, and people were searching for something deeper and more personal.

The passage says that although the mysteries failed adequately to satisfy this longing, they did prepare the way for the subsequent appearance of Jesus, who truly brought to this world the bread of life and the water thereof. Hunger is not itself food, but it makes one ready to receive food. The spiritual thirst deep in people's hearts made room for the gospel of Jesus to enter. God uses even imperfect religious efforts as preparation for a greater truth. This teaching gives us wisdom for the way we regard other religions and spiritual quests today. We see people seeking spiritual experience along many different paths. Rather than condemning this outright, we need eyes that recognize the real hunger within it. At the bottom of every religious quest is the soul's longing to find God, a longing that is also stirred by the indwelling Thought Adjuster.

At the same time, we must also have discernment. Emotionally stirring rites or mystical experiences are not in themselves spiritual growth. True religion shows itself in a personal relationship with God and in the loving service that flows from that relationship. The bread of life Jesus gave was not a mysterious rite but a life of doing the Father's will. This passage also prompts us to look at our own spiritual hunger. With what are we trying to satisfy that thirst? Are we not trying to fill it with busy schedules, possessions, recognition, or passing religious excitement? Such things comfort us for a while, but they cannot satisfy the soul.

When Jesus spoke to the Samaritan woman of water after which one would never thirst again, it was an answer to precisely this deep longing. He did not mock people's thirst but led it to its true source. We, too, can become people who respect our neighbors' spiritual longings and guide them to the source of life.

Today, let us look honestly at the deep longing within us and bring it to Jesus, the true bread of life. Only within the living relationship with the Father that he revealed will our hunger and thirst be fully satisfied.
d237.pr: Write down honestly what your heart has been hungering for lately, and bring it to the Father in prayer.

msg: In telling of Jesus' birth and infancy, Paper 122 first introduces his earthly parents, Joseph and Mary. Joseph was a Hebrew of the Hebrews, though he carried many non-Jewish racial strains, and Mary came of a line of ancestors notable in the racial history of Urantia. Today's passage explains why Gabriel chose these two as the bestowal parents.

According to the passage, of all couples living in Palestine at that time, Joseph and Mary possessed the most ideal combination of widespread racial connections and superior average of personality endowments. The key word here is average. They were not nobles, scholars, or of a priestly family. They were not especially brilliant or famous, but the most well-balanced among ordinary people. Why were such parents chosen? The passage states the reason plainly. It was the plan of Michael to appear on earth as an average man, that the common people might understand him and receive him. Had he been born in a palace or in the house of a high priest, ordinary people would have regarded him as someone from a world unlike their own. But because he was born in a carpenter's house and grew up in an ordinary family, he could become a brother to all.

This reveals a deep truth about the way God reveals himself. God does not seek to overwhelm and subdue human beings; he approaches them in ways they can understand and receive. That the Creator of a universe came as a baby in an ordinary Jewish family shows how near to us God wants to come. Greatness was revealed most clearly not in high places but in lowly ones. This teaching is a great encouragement to those of us who live ordinary lives. We often think that one must have special talent or position to be used by God. But God accomplished the greatest work through people like Joseph and Mary, ordinary yet faithful and well-balanced. Being ordinary is never being insignificant. On the contrary, it is a precious place from which to sympathize and connect with many people.

This passage also reminds us of the importance of the family. The place chosen for Michael to grow up as a human being was not a temple or a school but a family. Joseph's gentleness and conscientiousness and Mary's cheerfulness and determination played an important part in shaping Jesus' human character (see Paper 122, section 5). The fact that the divine Son grew up in the daily life of an ordinary family tells us that our family life, too, has holy meaning. We need not be disappointed that our lives are not glamorous. God works in ordinary kitchens, workshops, and back streets. When we live faithfully where we are now, with what we have now, he reveals himself through that life.

Interestingly, Joseph and Mary did not know from the beginning everything about the extraordinary work for which they had been chosen. They simply lived lives of honest daily work, loving each other and revering God. Readiness to be used by God takes shape in just such ordinary faithfulness. We, too, do not fully know what we are being prepared for now, but today's faithfulness prepares tomorrow's usefulness.

Today, let us receive our ordinary day with gratitude. As Joseph and Mary did, when we carry out small and ordinary tasks with faithfulness and love, our lives too will become places where God's will is done.
d238.pr: Choose one ordinary task for today and do it with care, as an offering to God.

d239.t: What He Received from His Parents
msg: The fifth section of Paper 122 depicts in detail the characters of Jesus' earthly parents, Joseph and Mary. Joseph was a mild-mannered man, extremely conscientious and faithful to the religious observances, quiet and thoughtful by temperament. Mary, on the other hand, was usually cheerful and optimistic, freely expressive of her feelings, and determined. Today's passage shows what Jesus inherited from these two parents.

According to the passage, Jesus derived much of his unusual gentleness and marvelous sympathetic understanding of human nature from his father Joseph. And he inherited his gift as a great teacher and his tremendous capacity for righteous indignation from his mother Mary. The Jesus we see in the Gospels, the tender Jesus who takes children into his arms and the resolute Jesus who drives the merchants out of the temple, is the temperament of these two parents blended within one personality.

The passage also says that in adult life Jesus was at times like his father, meditative and worshipful, sometimes showing apparent sadness, but more often he drove forward in the manner of his mother's optimistic and determined disposition. All in all, Mary's temperament tended to dominate his career. Jesus' human character did not arise in a vacuum; it was formed with real parents and in a real home environment. This shows how truly real Jesus' humanity was. He was not God merely appearing as a man. He was a genuine human being whose character was shaped through heredity, environment, and education. That is why he can be our example. He showed how one who grew up under the same conditions as we do can live doing the will of God fully.

This passage prompts us to reflect on our own characters. We, too, have inherited much from our parents. Some of it we are grateful for, and some of it we may wish to cast off. But Jesus' example shows that inherited temperament is not good or evil in itself; what matters is how we use it. Mary's strong feelings and determination became, in Jesus, righteous indignation and courageous teaching.

This passage also reminds us how great the influence of parents is. Joseph's capacity for sympathy and Mary's optimistic disposition left deep marks even on the Creator of a universe as he grew up as a human being. The character we show the next generation as parents, teachers, or elders remains long in their lives. What we show with our lives passes on more deeply than what we teach with words. Each of us has a different temperament. Some are quiet and thoughtful; others are lively and resolute. Just as these two temperaments were harmonized in Jesus, we too can shape our temperament into balance under the guidance of the Thought Adjuster. A character in which gentleness and resolve, meditation and action grow together is a mature spiritual personality. It is also worth remembering that Jesus' righteous indignation never flowed into personal grudge or revenge. That indignation was always for the sake of truth and the weak, and it was under the control of love. When a strong inherited temperament is refined by love, it becomes a power for justice.

Today, let us look back with gratitude on the character we have inherited and consider how we can use it for the will of God. Before it is an obstacle to overcome, our temperament is precious material we can offer to God.
d239.pr: Recall with gratitude one good trait you inherited from your parents, and use it for your neighbor today.

msg: Paper 123 tells of Jesus' early childhood, the period from his return from Egypt and settling in Nazareth until he entered school. The third section deals with the events of his sixth year, and today's passage shows how the young Jesus learned that year to manage his feelings. He made great progress in adjusting his strong feelings and vigorous impulses to the demands of family co-operation and home discipline.

The first thing to notice is that even the young Jesus had strong feelings and vigorous impulses. He was not a doll-like child without emotions. Like every other child, he wanted things and felt frustrated when they were denied. That the divine Son had real human feelings like these and learned to manage them shows how genuine his humanity was. The passage contrasts the two parents' ways of discipline. Mary was a loving mother but a fairly strict disciplinarian. Joseph, by contrast, would sit down with the boy and fully explain the real and underlying reasons for the necessity of disciplinary curtailment of personal desires in deference to the welfare and tranquillity of the entire family. So in many ways Joseph exerted the greater control over Jesus. When the situation had been explained to him, Jesus was always intelligently and willingly co-operative with his parents' wishes.

This holds deep wisdom about discipline. Commands alone can change a child's outward behavior, but they rarely change the heart. A child who is given the reasons, however, understands and accepts the rules for himself. Then obedience comes not from fear but from understanding and love. Later, in his public life, Jesus taught people by explaining and persuading rather than coercing, and he learned that way partly from Joseph. This teaching offers practical lessons for parents, teachers, and leaders. When we ask something of a child or of those under us, it is important to explain the reasons respectfully. It means treating the other as a personality endowed with intelligence. Explaining takes more time, but the cooperation formed in this way runs far deeper and lasts much longer.

This passage also speaks to our own self-discipline. We, too, have strong feelings and impulses. If we only suppress them by force, they are likely to explode someday. But when we understand why restraint is necessary and how it contributes to our own welfare and that of others, we can govern ourselves willingly. Managing feelings does not mean eliminating them but attuning them to a greater good. The ability to adjust personal desires to the welfare of the community is the heart of maturity. This ability, which the young Jesus learned at home, became the foundation of a life in which he would later wholly align his will with the will of God. The self-control learned under the discipline of a small household became the starting point of a cosmic obedience.

A child raised in a home where parents do not find the child's questions tiresome but answer them sincerely grows into a thinking person. Joseph's patient explanations cultivated in the young Jesus' mind a love of truth and the habit of asking why, and that habit later permeated all his teaching.

Today, when strong feelings surge within us, let us pause and explain to ourselves why we should manage them. And when we must lead others, let us show the patience to sit down with them, as Joseph did, and share the reasons.
d240.pr: When you ask something of someone today, calmly explain the reason and seek their cooperation instead of giving an order.

msg: The fifth section of Paper 123 tells of Jesus' school days in Nazareth. At seven he entered the synagogue school and studied the Hebrew scriptures, and at home he learned Aramaic and Greek. Today's passage sums up the whole of the education Jesus received under three sources and tells us which of them was his real education.

The first source is the home. Jesus received his moral training and spiritual culture chiefly in his own home. The daily piety and family prayers of Joseph and Mary, and the honesty and diligence his parents displayed, formed his moral foundation. The second source is the chazan, the synagogue teacher. Jesus secured much of his intellectual and theological education from him. The chazan recognized the boy's excellence and spent one evening a week with him, teaching him the scriptures in depth. But the passage calls the third source his real education. It was that equipment of mind and heart for the actual test of grappling with the difficult problems of life, and he obtained it by mingling with his fellow men. It was this close association with his fellow men, young and old, Jew and gentile, that afforded him the opportunity to know the human race.

Nazareth was a crossroads where caravans stopped to rest. In his father's shop and at the village spring, Jesus talked with travelers from every part of the world. From them he heard of the customs, thoughts, and concerns of other peoples. Meeting people in this way, he built up an understanding of humanity that cannot be learned from books. The last sentence of the passage is very striking: Jesus was highly educated in that he thoroughly understood men and devotedly loved them. Here the standard of education changes. Not degrees or the amount of knowledge, but how deeply one understands and loves people becomes the measure of true education. This teaching prompts us to reconsider our ideas of education and success today. We often prize academic credentials and qualifications, but these alone are not enough to pass life's real tests. Knowledge that does not understand people is cold, and ability that does not love people can be dangerous. Jesus' education was one in which knowledge and love grew together.

How, then, can we receive such an education? It begins with meeting people and listening sincerely to their stories. When we associate with people of different backgrounds, different ages, and different views, our understanding widens. The attitude of listening without prejudice and seeking understanding before judgment truly educates us. This passage also tells us where the remarkable understanding of human nature that Jesus showed in his public life came from. He could see into people's hearts and speak to each person the very word they needed because, from childhood, he had learned about humanity through close association with countless people. That learning began in love and was completed in love.

This education of Jesus continued after he became an adult. Whether building boats in Capernaum or traveling the Mediterranean, he always sought to know people and took a deep interest in their lives (see Paper 129). Learning about people is a lifelong task.

Today, let us regard the people around us as our teachers. Colleagues, neighbors, family, and even strangers we happen to meet can all teach us about humanity. As we strive to understand and love them, we too will grow, like Jesus, into truly educated people.
d241.pr: Today, listen to the whole story of someone whose background differs from yours, without judging.

d242.t: The Boy Who Would Not Fight
msg: Paper 124 tells of Jesus' later childhood, his growth from nine to thirteen years of age. The second section deals with his tenth year, and today's passage introduces the most unusual and outstanding trait that appeared during that time: his unwillingness to fight for his rights.

Jesus was a well-developed lad for his age, strong in body and keen in mind. Yet he was disinclined to defend himself even from injustice or when subjected to personal abuse. To his playfellows this seemed strange. That he did not fight, not because he lacked strength but while having it, was hard for them to understand. The passage also tells us why Jesus did not suffer much on account of this trait. Jacob, a neighbor boy one year older, so admired Jesus that he made it his business to see that no one was permitted to impose upon him. Uncouth youths who attacked Jesus, relying on his reputed docility, suffered swift retribution at the hands of Jacob, the stone mason's son. In this way heaven protected the boy Jesus through the friendship of a companion.

This refusal to assert his own rights became a trait running through Jesus' entire life. In his public life he taught people to turn the other cheek, and at the last, before an unjust trial and the cross, he did not defend himself. Its roots were already growing on the playground of a ten-year-old boy. Here we must be clear that this was neither servility nor weakness. When the rights of others were trampled, Jesus stepped forward resolutely and never hesitated to protect the weak. What he laid down was only the struggle on his own behalf. He spent on helping others the energy he might have spent defending himself.

The Urantia Book explains that the nonresistance Jesus taught in the Sermon on the Mount was not passive submission but an active and positive reaction to evil (see Paper 140). Not repaying evil with evil but overcoming it with good requires great inner strength and assurance. Only one who is assured of his worth in God can avoid clinging to his own rights. Let us consider how often in daily life we fight for our own rights. Are we not hurt by slight neglect, angered by small losses, and anxious to prove that we are right? Such quarrels wear us out and damage our relationships. Sometimes laying down our rights brings greater peace and freedom. This passage also shows the beauty of friendship. Jacob may not have understood Jesus, but he admired and protected him. Near us, too, are gentle people who need to be guarded from harm. We are sometimes called, like Jacob, to be a shield for others.

This attitude of Jesus was possible not because he was timid but because he enjoyed a deep security in God. His consciousness of being a beloved son of the heavenly Father kept the insults of others from shaking his being. When we are assured that our worth is already settled in God, whatever others may do to us, we too can be freed from the compulsion of self-defense.

Today, when someone treats us unfairly, let us pause and recall the way of Jesus before striking back at once. If we are assured that we are safe in God, we can be free from the struggle to prove ourselves.
d242.pr: Today, when you want to insist on your rights over some trifle, gladly yield once and choose peace.

msg: The fourth section of Paper 124 deals with Jesus' twelfth year. During this time he spent his last year of schooling, and his consciousness of his mission was steadily growing. At the same time, differences began to appear between his personal views and the established beliefs of his parents. Today's passage shows the deep inner conflict the boy Jesus went through at that time and how he resolved it.

According to the passage, Jesus suffered great mental distress as the result of his constant effort to adjust his personal views of religious practices and social amenities to the established beliefs of his parents. His supreme conflict was between two great commands. The one was: “⟦Q 124:4.9⟧Be loyal to the dictates of your highest convictions of truth and righteousness.⟦/Q⟧” The other was: “⟦Q 124:4.9⟧Honor your father and mother, for they have given you life and the nurture thereof.⟦/Q⟧”

This conflict was very real. Jesus understood God as a loving Father, but his parents followed the customs and interpretations of traditional Judaism. He wanted to be true to his convictions, yet he also wanted to respect and obey his parents. Because both were right values, finding a way between them was not easy. What is remarkable is that Jesus never shirked this responsibility. He chose neither the easy way of abandoning his convictions and obeying his parents unconditionally nor the easy way of ignoring his parents and insisting only on his own convictions. Instead, he made the necessary daily adjustments between loyalty to his personal convictions and duty toward his family. It was not a single decision but an everyday effort.

And that effort bore fruit. The passage says he achieved the satisfaction of effecting an increasingly harmonious blending of personal convictions and family obligations into a masterful concept of group solidarity based upon loyalty, fairness, tolerance, and love. The conflict did not break him but made him a more mature and balanced person. This teaching touches the struggles many people face today. Growing children come to think differently from their parents, and on the path of faith, too, they may arrive at an understanding different from their family's. At such times we easily swing to the extremes of cutting off the family or abandoning our own conscience. Jesus' example shows a third way: seeking harmony between them with patience and love.

This way involves pain. The passage frankly says that even Jesus suffered great mental distress. But that pain is not in vain. In striving to harmonize differing values, we learn tolerance, learn to understand another's position, and learn to speak the truth in love. This passage also teaches that being true to one's convictions does not mean disregarding others. True conviction goes hand in hand with love. One who holds to truth does not force his views on others but keeps his relationships with respect and patience. The generosity Jesus later showed in his public life was already growing in these adjustments of his boyhood. This conflict of the boy Jesus is also evidence of how deeply he loved his family. Had he not loved them, there would have been no conflict. Our own conflicts, too, arise from the effort to hold fast to both love and truth.

Today, when we differ in our thinking from our family or those close to us, let us accept it not as a conflict to be cut off but as an opportunity to learn harmony. Seeking each day a way that stays true to conviction without losing love is the path Jesus walked.
d243.pr: Think of a family member whose views differ from yours, and look for a way to respect them while keeping your convictions.

d244.t: The Father Who Does Not Pour Out Wrath
msg: Paper 125 tells of the twelve-year-old Jesus' first visit to Jerusalem. He went up with his parents to the Passover feast to be consecrated as a son of the law, and there for the first time he saw the great temple and its splendid ceremonies. Today's passage contains the moving confession Jesus made to his father Joseph just after the temple visit.

According to the passage, many of the temple rituals very touchingly impressed his sense of the beautiful and the symbolic. Yet he was always disappointed by the explanations of the real meanings of these ceremonies that his parents offered. In particular, Jesus simply would not accept explanations of worship and religious devotion which involved belief in the wrath of God or the anger of the Almighty. The idea that God's wrath must be appeased by bloody sacrifices did not fit the God he knew.

When Joseph became mildly insistent that he acknowledge acceptance of the orthodox Jewish beliefs, Jesus, looking appealingly into his father's eyes, said: “⟦Q 125:0.6⟧My father, it cannot be true — the Father in heaven cannot so regard his erring children on earth. The heavenly Father cannot love his children less than you love me.⟦/Q⟧” He knew that his earthly father would never pour out wrath upon him; how much more, then, must the heavenly Father be filled with goodness and overflowing with mercy. This confession already contains the heart of the gospel Jesus would later proclaim to the whole world. God is not a wrathful judge but a loving Father. His love is infinitely greater than the best love of human parents. Jesus learned this truth not from a theology textbook but in his own home, through Joseph's love. A good father's love became a window for understanding the heavenly Father.

In many places the Urantia Book explains that the concept of God as a deity of wrath and vengeance arose from mankind's primitive fear. The concepts of sacrifice and atonement are traces of a long religious evolution that regarded God as a being who had to be appeased (see Paper 89). Jesus went beyond this old religion of fear and opened the way to a religion of love and trust. This teaching prompts us to examine our own faith today. Are we perhaps still living our religious lives in fear of God, trying to avoid his wrath? Do we worry about punishment every time we make a mistake, or feel that we must offer something to earn God's love? Jesus' confession sets us free from such fears.

Of course, God does not take sin lightly. But his response comes not from wrath but from love, as correction and restoration. Just as a good parent corrects an erring child but never hates the child, the heavenly Father does not withdraw his love from us even in the face of our wrongdoing. This passage also holds deep meaning for the role of parents. Joseph's love became the foundation for Jesus' understanding of God. The love we show our children and those around us affects how they will imagine God. Our love can become a mirror reflecting the love of God. This twelve-year-old's confession is like the first sounding of the gospel that would later set countless hearts free. The parable of the father who runs out to welcome the prodigal son, too, may be said to have grown from this conviction of his early years.
Today, let us look upon God anew, not as one who is wrathful but as a loving Father. And trusting that love, let us come to him without fear.
d244.pr: If there is any part of you that fears God, write it down and tell it honestly to the loving Father.

msg: The last part of Paper 125 tells of how his parents found Jesus after he had spent three days discussing with the teachers in the temple at Jerusalem, and of what followed. When Mary reproached him, asking why he had done this, Jesus answered, “Did you not know that I must be about my Father's business?” Yet he soon returned to Nazareth with his parents and lived in obedience to them. Today's passage sums up the attitude Jesus showed during this period.

According to the passage, Jesus in his mind would many times refuse to consent to the well-intentioned but misguided efforts of his parents. They sought to dictate the course of his thinking and to establish the plan of his work on earth. Mary expected him to become the Messiah of the Jews, and Joseph hoped he would be educated as a rabbi. Jesus knew that such plans did not agree with the Father's will.

But the passage goes on to say that in every manner consistent with his dedication to the doing of his Paradise Father's will, he did most gracefully conform to the desires of his earthly father and to the usages of his family in the flesh. Even when he could not consent, he would do everything possible to conform. He clearly distinguished between matters of principle and matters of method. The passage describes Jesus as an artist in the matter of adjusting his dedication to duty to his obligations of family loyalty and social service. The word artist is beautiful. It means that this is not something to be solved by mechanical rules but creative work requiring delicate sensitivity, wisdom, and love. Knowing when to bend and when to stand firm is an art.

This attitude helps us avoid a trap into which spiritual people easily fall. Those who claim to follow God's will sometimes disregard the people around them, forsake the legitimate expectations of their families, and insist only on their own way. But because Jesus held the supreme dedication to God, he was all the more able to yield gladly in small matters. One who is firm in essentials can be generous in nonessentials. This wisdom is much needed in our relationships today. At home, at work, and in our communities we meet the expectations and customs of others. We need not oppose them all. As long as it does not violate conscience and the will of God, conforming out of consideration for others is an expression of love. Not quarreling over trifles while being faithful in great things: this is the mark of a mature person.

Conformity, moreover, is different from servility. Jesus did not abandon the convictions in his heart, and he never compromised his dedication to the Father's business. He simply respected his family and society in the way he expressed that dedication. That is why his conformity had dignity. Jesus refined this art over eighteen years in Nazareth while caring for his family. That time was also preparation for his public life. His ability to respect many kinds of people and customs without losing the truth enabled him to reach people of every class. Even right after he had become strongly conscious of his mission in the temple, Jesus did not refuse to return to the ordinary daily life of Nazareth. The sight of one who has received a great realization humbly returning to everyday life and carrying out small duties is a beautiful sign of spiritual maturity.

Today, let us also seek the wisdom to distinguish principle from method. May it be a day of holding firmly to what must be kept, gladly yielding what can be yielded, and getting along with people with grace.
d245.pr: Consider whether something you are insisting on today is a matter of principle or of method, and if it is method, gladly yield.

msg: Paper 126 deals with Jesus' fourteenth and fifteenth years, the two most crucial years of his life. The second section tells of Joseph's sudden death. While working on the governor's residence at Sepphoris, Joseph fell from a high derrick, was gravely injured, and died. Today's passage shows what that tragedy meant to the fourteen-year-old Jesus.

The passage says that it came just at the time when prospects were good and the future looked bright. The family's circumstances were improving, and plans were being made for Jesus' education. Then an apparently cruel hand struck down the head of the household, and every plan was demolished. In our lives, too, unexpected loss often comes at the most hopeful moment. The carpenter lad, now just past fourteen, had to shoulder two burdens at once. One was to fulfill the commission of his heavenly Father to reveal the divine nature on earth. The other was to care for his widowed mother and seven brothers and sisters, and another yet to be born. He became the sole support and comfort of this family.

A notable expression in the passage is that these things were permitted. The passage says that these occurrences of the natural order of events on Urantia were permitted so that Jesus would assume early these heavy but highly educational and disciplinary responsibilities. Heaven did not cause Joseph's death; by not intervening in the natural course of things, it allowed that experience to serve Jesus' growth.

This gives a deep understanding of suffering. The Urantia Book does not teach that God deliberately sends accidents and tragedies (see Paper 123, section 4). But when such things happen, God helps us grow through them. In his grief over the loss of his father, Jesus became the head of the household, a father to his brothers and sisters, and the protector of his mother. That experience made him a true brother to all who suffer. How Jesus accepted this burden also matters. The next paragraph tells us that he willingly accepted the responsibility that had suddenly come upon him and carried it out faithfully to the end. He did not complain or run away. He laid down his own dreams and plans and gave his whole heart to caring for the family entrusted to him. For that was the Father's will at that moment.

In our lives, too, there are times when an unwanted burden is suddenly laid upon us. A family member's illness, a sudden loss, an unexpected responsibility shatters our plans. At such times we ask why this has happened to me. Jesus' example shows that a more important question than that is how I can be faithful in this situation. And let us remember that the burden is never in vain. The years Jesus spent caring for his family in Nazareth taught him the realities of human life and made him a teacher full of sympathy and wisdom. In the hands of the Thought Adjuster, our burdens, too, become material for shaping character. After Joseph's death, Jesus must have comforted his grieving mother, held his young brothers and sisters, and at night prayed alone, asking the Father for strength. That picture is a quiet comfort to every family going through loss.

Today, let us look upon the heavy responsibilities we bear with trust instead of resentment. Even within that burden the Father is with us, and through it he is making us grow into deeper and broader people.
d246.pr: Recall one heavy responsibility you are carrying now, and write down what you are learning through it.
